dek: Audible let people buy books to listen to, downloaded from the web, years before most owned a player.
lede: The iPod was still two years away, so Audible built its own player. The little device carried books, magazines, and radio programs that customers downloaded from the web, by the title or by subscription. When the New Jersey company went public in July 1999, most audiobooks still lived on cassettes and CDs. Home internet ran over dial-up modems. Audible was selling a habit that the hardware had yet to catch up with.

sections.heading: A Library for the Ear
sections.body: Don Katz, a journalist and author, founded Audible in New Jersey in 1995. His bet was that spoken word belonged on the internet, off the plastic of tapes and discs. The company signed rights to books and periodicals and recorded much of its own catalog. Listeners would pay by the title or by subscription and play a book whenever they liked. In 1997 Audible shipped the Audible Mobile Player, a clumsy device fed by slow downloads.

sections.heading: Rescued by iTunes
sections.body: Audible priced its offering at $9 a share in July 1999. The years after were hard. When the dot-com bubble burst, the stock fell far below its offer price. Then, in 2003, Audible signed a deal to supply audiobooks to Apple's iTunes Store. At last the company had the device it had always needed. Amazon bought Audible in 2008 for about $300 million, and Audible became the default place to buy an audiobook.

cover.theme: a lute player (music for the ear)

tagline: The State Website That Paid for Itself
dek: NIC let people deal with their state government online, and the states paid nothing upfront for the websites.
lede: Lawyers, insurers, and lenders paid for NIC's state websites, one small fee at a time. The Kansas company offered states a simple deal. It would build and run their official websites at no upfront cost. It would earn its money from fees on services like driving records and business filings. In 1999 most dealings with a state still meant a line at an office counter. NIC went public that July with several states signed up.

sections.heading: Free to Kansas
sections.body: Jeffery Fraser started the business in Kansas in the early 1990s as the Kansas Information Consortium. The model paid for itself. A state gave NIC a contract, and NIC paid to build the portal. Fees from frequent users, often lawyers, insurers, and lenders, covered the cost. That removed the biggest obstacle for state agencies, which rarely had technology budgets to spare. Each new state contract became a long-running source of revenue.

sections.heading: Quiet Growth, State by State
sections.body: NIC priced its offering at $12 a share in July 1999. Like many internet stocks, it fell hard in 2000. The business underneath kept growing. State by state, NIC added portals and services, betting that public services would follow commerce onto the web. In the end it ran official websites for a large share of American states. In 2021 Tyler Technologies, a maker of software for local governments, bought NIC for about $2.3 billion.

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2014 ($4.3B)
dek: TIBCO let a company's computer systems share news the instant it happened, a trick learned on Wall Street.
lede: TIBCO's name stood for "The Information Bus," software built for trading floors where a delay of seconds cost money. The bus let separate computer systems publish and receive messages the instant something changed. It began on Wall Street in the late 1980s. By 1999 large companies of every kind had the same problem across their own systems, and the web made it more urgent. When TIBCO went public that July, Reuters owned a majority of it.

sections.heading: From Teknekron to Everyone
sections.body: Vivek Ranadivé built the information bus at his earlier company, Teknekron Software Systems. Reuters bought Teknekron in 1994. In 1997 TIBCO Software became its own company, so it could sell the technology beyond finance. The bet was that every business would need what traders needed: data that arrived as events happened, instead of in nightly batches. TIBCO called this "the event-driven enterprise" and sold it to banks, telecom companies, and manufacturers.

sections.heading: Vista, Then Citrix
sections.body: TIBCO priced its offering at $15 a share in July 1999. The stock climbed sharply through the following year and fell with the rest of the market in 2001. The company stayed profitable and grew by acquisition, adding integration, analytics, and visualization products. In 2014 Vista Equity Partners took TIBCO private for about $4.3 billion. TIBCO later became part of Cloud Software Group, alongside Citrix.

cover.theme: a fast mail coach (the information bus)

dek: Ask Jeeves let people type questions in plain English and get answers from a cartoon butler.
lede: Ask Jeeves borrowed a valet from P. G. Wodehouse's fiction and put him in charge of a search engine. Early search engines made people think like librarians and type keywords. Ask Jeeves let them type a question, as they would to a person. Editors behind the scenes matched common questions to good answers. When the company went public on July 1, 1999, the web was full of new users who found keyword search confusing.

sections.heading: Plain English Over Keywords
sections.body: Garrett Gruener, a venture capitalist, and David Warthen, a software engineer, started the company in Berkeley in 1996. Their bet was that plain language would beat keywords. The system paired software that parsed questions with a large library of answers that people had written and checked. The cartoon butler on the home page gave the service a personality. By 1999 Jeeves was one of the best-known faces online.

sections.heading: Google Changes the Question
sections.body: Ask Jeeves priced its offering at $14 a share on July 1, 1999, and the stock soared on its first day of trading. Google soon showed that good ranking mattered more than plain-language parsing. Ask Jeeves bought the Teoma search engine in 2001 to keep up. IAC acquired the company in 2005 for about $1.85 billion. The butler retired in 2006, and the service carried on as Ask.com.

cover.theme: a valet with a coffee pot (the butler)
cover.artwork: Study of Valet with Coffee Pot

dek: E-Loan let home buyers see and compare mortgage rates and fees online, out in the open.
lede: E-Loan showed borrowers the fees it charged, and in the mortgage business of 1999 that was unusual. Buying a house then meant a broker, a stack of paper, and fees few borrowers understood. E-Loan put the process on the web. Borrowers could compare rates from many lenders, apply online, and track their loan toward closing. E-Loan went public in June 1999, betting that open pricing would win buyers who felt brokers kept them in the dark.

sections.heading: Two Brokers Open the Books
sections.body: Chris Larsen and Janina Pawlowski had worked together in mortgage brokerage. In 1996 they founded E-Loan in the San Francisco Bay Area. Their bet was transparency. E-Loan showed borrowers the rates it got and the fees it charged. It still earned its money as a broker, like the firms it competed with. The internet let it serve borrowers anywhere, at a lower cost than a branch office.

sections.heading: A Refinancing Boom Arrives
sections.body: E-Loan priced its offering at $14 a share in June 1999. The stock fell steeply when the bubble burst. The business survived, and it later turned a profit as low interest rates drove a refinancing boom. In 2005 Popular, Inc., the Puerto Rico banking group, acquired E-Loan. Chris Larsen later co-founded two more companies: the lending marketplace Prosper, and then Ripple.

tagline: The Post Office in Your Printer
dek: Stamps.com let people buy official U.S. postage online and print it at home, with no trip to the post office.
lede: Every stamp Stamps.com sold was a barcode from an ordinary printer, proof to the Postal Service that someone had paid. For more than a century, postage had meant a trip to the post office or a leased postage meter. In 1999 the U.S. Postal Service began testing postage bought over the internet. Stamps.com was one of the first companies approved to sell it. It went public that June, aiming at small businesses and home offices that mailed often.

sections.heading: Goodbye to the Meter
sections.body: The bet was that a printer and an internet connection could replace the postage meter. Small offices that mailed often had little reason to lease one if their printer could do the job. Stamps.com handled the security the Postal Service demanded. It encoded each printed stamp with a barcode that proved it was paid for. Customers paid a monthly fee for the software and service. In return they got no lines, no meter lease, and postage ready at any hour.

sections.heading: Shipping Labels for Online Sellers
sections.body: Stamps.com priced its offering at $11 a share in June 1999. The stock rose fast, then fell hard in the crash that followed. The company cut costs and outlasted its rivals. It found steady growth in shipping labels for online sellers, and it bought ShipStation and other shipping tools as e-commerce grew. In 2021 Thoma Bravo took Stamps.com private for about $6.6 billion.

cover.theme: a woman with a letter (the mail)

tagline: The Router That Took On Cisco
dek: Juniper built the fast routers that carried internet traffic for big carriers, and gave Cisco its first serious rival.
lede: Juniper's first router had shipped only months before the company went public, and carriers were already lining up to test it. In 1999 internet traffic was doubling at a pace that strained the routers at its core. Nearly all of those machines came from Cisco, and many were general-purpose computers doing a specialized job. Juniper built a router for the backbone from scratch, with custom chips that forwarded packets at full line speed.

sections.heading: A Router Split in Two
sections.body: Pradeep Sindhu, a computer scientist from Xerox PARC, founded Juniper in 1996. His bet was that the internet core needed purpose-built hardware, in place of software running on general processors. Juniper split the router into two parts. A control plane made the routing decisions. A forwarding engine in silicon moved the packets. Its M40 router, released in 1998, handled far more traffic per box than competitors and won early customers among large carriers.

sections.heading: A Quarter Century Against Cisco
sections.body: Juniper priced its offering at $34 a share in June 1999, and it became one of the most successful offerings of the era. The stock soared through 2000 as carriers raced to build capacity. Then it fell sharply when the telecom bubble burst. Juniper survived as Cisco's main rival in carrier and data center networking for a quarter century. In 2025 Hewlett Packard Enterprise completed its purchase of Juniper for about $14 billion.

cover.theme: a cypress, kin of the juniper

tagline: Payments Born in a Software Store
dek: CyberSource let online stores take credit cards from strangers safely, checking every order for fraud.
lede: CyberSource began as the payment system inside software.net, an early online software store. The store had built tools to accept cards and spot fraud, and other merchants needed the same tools. In 1999 any business that wanted to sell online had to work out how to take a stranger's credit card and know it was real. CyberSource sold the answer as a service. It went public that June.

sections.heading: Plumbing for Online Commerce
sections.body: William McKiernan started CyberSource in 1996 inside software.net. A merchant's website passed each order to CyberSource. CyberSource authorized the card, checked for fraud, and handled tax and export rules. It was one of the first companies to sell payment processing over the internet to other internet companies. The bet was that the plumbing of online commerce would be a business of its own. CyberSource charged per transaction, so it grew as online shopping grew.

sections.heading: Visa Buys the Plumbing
sections.body: CyberSource priced its offering at $11 a share in June 1999. The stock climbed fast and then collapsed in the dot-com crash. The company kept its core business and stayed independent. In 2007 it bought Authorize.Net, adding thousands of small merchants. Visa acquired CyberSource in 2010 for about $2 billion. The name lives on as Visa's platform for online payments.

cover.artwork: The Merchant (Sho) from the series Beauties Illustrating the Four Classes

dek: Ariba let big companies buy everything from pens to computers online, with fewer forms and phone calls.
lede: Ariba took the purchase order, a dull back-office form, and turned it into a Wall Street star. In the 1990s big companies bought pens and computers through paper forms and phone calls. Ariba moved that buying to the web. Employees chose items from an online catalog, managers approved them, and orders went to suppliers electronically. When Ariba went public in June 1999, business-to-business commerce was the hottest idea on Wall Street, and Ariba was its clearest example.

sections.heading: Fortune in the Back Office
sections.body: Keith Krach and a group of co-founders started Ariba in Silicon Valley in 1996. The bet was that procurement, a dull back-office task, was a large market waiting for the web. Ariba's software cut the cost of processing a purchase order. It also steered spending toward preferred suppliers. Ariba built a network as well, so a supplier could connect once and reach many buyers.

sections.heading: The Network Outlasts the Bubble
sections.body: Ariba priced its offering at $23 a share in June 1999, and the stock soared on its first day of trading. At its peak the company was worth tens of billions of dollars. It lost most of that value when the bubble burst. Ariba cut costs and refocused on its supplier network, which became its lasting strength. SAP bought Ariba in 2012 for about $4.3 billion.

cover.theme: a harbor (where buyers and sellers meet)
cover.artwork: Ships in the Harbor at Sète

tagline: Seven-Dollar Shares in a Trading Boom
dek: onlinetradinginc.com let investors buy and sell stocks on their own over the internet, for low commissions.
lede: onlinetradinginc.com sold its own shares for $7 apiece in June 1999, one of the smaller deals of a busy summer. Online trading was a defining story of the bull market. Millions of people opened accounts with internet brokers, and low commissions drew a new crowd of active traders. This small Florida brokerage sold self-directed trading through its website. It went public hoping to grow as more investors moved their accounts online.

sections.heading: Lean, Cheap, and Fast
sections.body: The bet was simple. As trading moved to the web, a lean online broker could win customers on price and service. Like its competitors, the firm earned money from commissions on each trade. Its revenue rose and fell with the market's mood. Smaller brokers like this one faced well-funded rivals that spent heavily on advertising to win accounts. Price and speed were its main selling points.

sections.heading: When the Volume Dried Up
sections.body: onlinetradinginc.com priced its offering at $7 a share in June 1999. Its underwriter, Werbel-Roth Securities, sold 2,587,500 shares, counting the extra shares it sold on July 1. Trading volume fell when the market turned in 2000. That put pressure on every online broker that lived on commissions. In the years that followed, the industry consolidated quickly. Larger firms bought up smaller ones and fought over price.

cover.theme: speculators trading at the Palais Royal
cover.artwork: Study for The Speculators at the Palais Royal

dek: BackWeb sent news, files, and software updates to computers in the background, so people never had to fetch them.
lede: BackWeb slipped files onto computers through spare network capacity, so people kept working while the data arrived. It was a leading system for "push," one of the most hyped ideas on the early web. Instead of making people visit websites, push software sent news, updates, and files straight to their computers. By the time the Israeli company went public in June 1999, the consumer hype had faded. BackWeb sold to companies that needed to reach their own employees.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and BRM
sections.body: Eli Barkat co-founded BackWeb in 1995 with backing from BRM, the Israeli technology group he ran with his brother Nir. The bet was that the web should come to the user. BackWeb's software used spare network capacity to deliver content quietly in the background. Users kept working while the files arrived. Large companies used it to send sales materials, software patches, and alerts across their networks.

sections.heading: Offline Work for Laptops
sections.body: BackWeb priced its offering at $12 a share in June 1999. The stock rose with the market. Then the bubble burst, companies cut spending, and the stock fell. BackWeb moved toward software that let laptop users work offline with web applications. In 2003 Eli Barkat resigned as chief executive and went back to BRM Capital, the venture fund he had started with Nir. BackWeb stayed a small company in the years that followed.

cover.theme: a spider's web (the web that comes to you)
cover.artwork: Woman with Spider's Web Between Bare Trees

dek: F5 kept busy websites online by spreading each surge of visitors across many servers.
lede: F5 Networks named itself after the strongest class of tornado, and it sold shelter from a storm of web traffic. In 1999 the busiest websites were learning that one server was never enough. Visitors arrived in surges, and a single overloaded machine could take a whole site down. F5 sold a box that sat in front of a group of servers. It sent each visitor to the server best able to respond. F5 went public that June.

sections.heading: BIG-IP in Seattle
sections.body: Michael Almquist and Jeff Hussey founded F5 in Seattle in 1996. The bet was that websites would become critical services that could never fail. Their product, BIG-IP, checked the health of each server and routed traffic around failures. It turned a rack of ordinary machines into one reliable website. Online retailers, portals, and banks were among the early customers. They needed their sites up at every hour of the day.

sections.heading: Its Customers Vanished, F5 Stayed
sections.body: F5 priced its offering at $10 a share in June 1999. The stock climbed through the boom. In 2000 and 2001 it fell sharply, as many of its dot-com customers disappeared. F5 rebuilt around large enterprises and service providers. It added security and application delivery features. F5 became one of the long-term survivors of its class, and it remains a public company today, trading on the Nasdaq as FFIV.

dek: Network Access Solutions sold businesses in the Mid-Atlantic fast, always-on internet over their existing phone lines.
lede: A 1996 law let Network Access Solutions rent the old Bell copper lines and turn them into broadband for businesses. The Telecommunications Act opened the local phone network to upstart carriers. A new technology, DSL, let the old copper carry fast internet. Network Access Solutions was one of these competitive carriers. The Virginia company focused on businesses in the Bell Atlantic region. It went public in June 1999 to pay for a rapid build-out.

sections.heading: Faster Than Dial-Up
sections.body: The bet was that small and medium businesses would pay for always-on internet. It would be far faster than dial-up and cheaper than a leased line. Network Access Solutions placed its equipment in phone company central offices. It sold service directly and through internet providers. Growth required heavy spending before customers arrived. That made the business dependent on open capital markets.

sections.heading: When the Money Ran Out
sections.body: Network Access Solutions priced its offering at $12 a share in June 1999. When the telecom bubble burst in 2000, the money that funded carriers like it dried up. In June 2002 the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. In early 2003 DSL.net bought its network assets and business customers. The network lived on. The company that built it joined a long list of DSL carriers that failed when the money ran out.

cover.theme: a copper mine canyon (old copper lines)
cover.artwork: Bingham Canon, Telegraph Mine, near Salt Lake Utah

fate: Sold its operations to Charter Communications, 2002
dek: High Speed Access brought fast cable internet to small towns and rural areas that big cities already had.
lede: High Speed Access had Paul Allen's money behind it and an Allen company, Charter, as its biggest partner. In 1999 cable-modem internet was the fastest way online at home, but it reached mostly big cities. Small-town cable systems often lacked the partners and capital to offer it. High Speed Access upgraded those systems, ran the service, and handled support. It split the revenue with the cable operator. It went public in June 1999, backed by Allen's Vulcan Ventures.

sections.heading: A Partner in Allen's Orbit
sections.body: The bet was that broadband would spread beyond the big cities, and that someone would need to bring it there. High Speed Access offered small cable operators a turnkey service, so they could skip building their own technical teams. Its largest partner was Charter Communications, another company in Paul Allen's orbit. That tie was both a strength and a risk. In the end, Charter would also be its buyer.

sections.heading: Charter Buys the Network
sections.body: High Speed Access priced its offering at $13 a share in June 1999. The model needed heavy spending in each new town. Losses mounted when capital grew scarce in 2000. In 2001 the company agreed to sell its operations to Charter. Charter closed the purchase in February 2002, paying $81.1 million in cash and taking on some liabilities. High Speed Access was left with little more than cash and the task of winding down its affairs.

dek: EDGAR Online turned free but clumsy SEC filings into searchable data and alerts that investors could use.
lede: Every SEC filing became free to read in the mid-1990s, and EDGAR Online built a business selling them anyway. The raw documents were long, plain text, and hard to search. EDGAR Online added alerts, search tools, and data pulled from financial statements. In 1999 a new wave of individual investors was reading filings for the first time. EDGAR Online went public that May, aiming to be their guide.

sections.heading: Order From Public Data
sections.body: Susan and Marc Strausberg founded the company in Connecticut in 1995. The SEC's own EDGAR database supplied the raw material for free. The bet was that public data became valuable once someone organized it. EDGAR Online tagged, indexed, and delivered the filings faster than the government site, in friendlier formats. It sold subscriptions to investors, lawyers, and analysts. It also licensed its data to websites and financial firms.

sections.heading: XBRL Becomes the Rule
sections.body: EDGAR Online priced its offering at $9.50 a share in May 1999. The company never grew large. It spent years building tools for XBRL, a tagged data format for financial statements. The SEC later required that format, so the machine-readable data EDGAR Online had promoted became a regulatory requirement. In 2012 RR Donnelley, the financial printing company, acquired EDGAR Online. Its products joined RR Donnelley's financial services business, and the EDGAR Online brand continued for a time.

cover.artwork: The Raven on the Bust of Pallas

dek: Redback made the gear that let phone companies sign up and manage millions of new broadband customers.
lede: Every new DSL customer had to be logged in, given an address, and routed to the right internet provider, and Redback built the box that did it. In 1999 phone companies were rolling out DSL and needed a way to handle the flood. Redback's Subscriber Management System sat at the edge of the carrier network. Redback went public in May 1999, as broadband moved from trial to mass market.

sections.heading: A New Layer of Network
sections.body: Gaurav Garg and Asher Waldfogel founded Redback in Silicon Valley in 1996. The bet was that broadband would create a new layer of the network, between the access lines and the internet core. That layer would need its own equipment. Redback's SMS product won quick adoption among carriers deploying DSL. It became one of the most celebrated networking start-ups of its moment.

sections.heading: Siara, Bankruptcy, Ericsson
sections.body: Redback priced its offering at $23 a share in May 1999, and the stock leapt on its first day. That same year it bought Siara Systems in a stock deal worth billions. Its value soared, and then the telecom crash erased most of it. In 2003 Redback restructured through a prepackaged bankruptcy and emerged as a smaller company. Ericsson acquired Redback in 2007 for about $2.1 billion.

tagline: The Catalog That Became Gossip Girl
dek: Alloy sold clothes to teenage girls through a mailed catalog and kept them coming back with a website.
lede: The company behind Gossip Girl and Pretty Little Liars started as a clothing catalog for teenage girls. In 1999 teenagers were the first generation to grow up online, and marketers wanted to reach them. Alloy mailed a fashion catalog to millions of homes, aimed at girls aged roughly 10 to 24. Its website offered quizzes, chat, and content written in their voice. The catalog paid the bills, and the website built loyalty. Alloy went public in May 1999.

sections.heading: A Store and a Hangout
sections.body: Matt Diamond and James Johnson founded Alloy in New York in 1996. The bet was that one brand could be both a store and a gathering place for young people. Alloy used its website to grow its customer list. It used its catalog to turn that audience into sales. Advertisers that wanted to reach teens also paid for access to the community. Wall Street saw Alloy as the company that understood teens on the web.

sections.heading: The Book Packager Pays Off
sections.body: Alloy priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999. As the dot-com market cooled, it moved toward marketing and media services. It bought magazines, school marketing programs, and a book packager. That unit, Alloy Entertainment, developed series such as Gossip Girl and Pretty Little Liars. A business that began with a catalog and a chat room had become a media company. In 2010 ZelnickMedia took Alloy private.

dek: Copper Mountain sold the equipment that let new phone companies turn ordinary copper lines into fast internet.
lede: Copper Mountain's biggest buyers, Covad and NorthPoint, were DSL upstarts, and the company rose and fell with them. These new phone companies rented copper lines from the old monopolies and installed their own equipment in central offices. Copper Mountain made that equipment, the access concentrators that turned plain copper into broadband. When it went public in May 1999, its customers were the fastest-growing carriers of the moment, and its sales were rising quickly.

sections.heading: Paying by the Square Foot
sections.body: Copper Mountain was founded in 1996. The bet was that the copper already running into every home and office could carry far more than voice. Its systems packed many DSL lines into a small space. That mattered in crowded central offices, where carriers paid by the square foot. Covad and NorthPoint, two of the largest new DSL carriers, were major buyers.

sections.heading: Sold for $10 Million
sections.body: Copper Mountain priced its offering at $21 a share in May 1999, and the stock rose sharply through the following year. Then its customers began to fail. When the new carriers went bankrupt or slowed in 2000 and 2001, Copper Mountain's sales collapsed. In 2005 Tut Systems acquired the company in a stock deal valued at about $10 million. Tut wanted its engineers for internet television.

dek: Portal Software let internet and phone companies bill millions of customers for web access, email, and content.
lede: Old phone billing systems knew how to charge for minutes of voice calls, and little else. In 1999 internet providers needed to bill for web access, email accounts, and content. Portal Software sold a billing platform built for the internet. It tracked usage, applied complex pricing plans, and produced bills for millions of customers. Portal went public in May 1999, promising to be the cash register behind every carrier's new online services.

sections.heading: A Consulting Firm Since 1985
sections.body: John Little started the company in 1985 as a consulting firm, and it built billing tools for early online services. The bet was that internet services would need flexible, real-time billing, and that carriers would buy it instead of building it. Portal's Infranet product ran on standard servers and could change pricing quickly. Carriers launching new services valued that speed, because new products appeared every month.

sections.heading: Restatements, Then Oracle
sections.body: Portal priced its offering at $14 a share in May 1999, and its stock rose sharply in the boom. When carriers cut spending in 2001, Portal's sales fell and its losses grew. Accounting problems later forced Portal to restate its results, and the Nasdaq delisted its stock. Oracle acquired Portal in 2006. Its billing software became part of Oracle's communications products.

cover.artwork: Coventry, St. Mary's Hall, Entrance Gateway

tagline: An eService Desk in New Hampshire
dek: Silknet let big companies answer customers by web, email, and phone from one shared record.
lede: Silknet sold itself for Kana stock worth billions of dollars, then watched most of that value vanish within the year. The New Hampshire company had a timely product. By 1999 customers expected answers by email and on the web, and most companies had no good way to track those conversations. Silknet's platform, eService, gave support agents and customers one shared view of questions, answers, and history. Silknet went public in May 1999.

sections.heading: Answers First, Agents Second
sections.body: The bet was that customer service would become a web business, and that companies would need software to run it. Silknet's platform let customers find answers on their own. It passed harder questions to human agents with the full history attached. It sold to large companies that handled huge volumes of support requests. Large firms in telecom, technology, and finance were among the buyers.

sections.heading: Signed at the Peak
sections.body: Silknet priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999, and the stock climbed quickly in the boom. In 2000 Kana Communications agreed to buy Silknet in an all-stock deal valued at billions of dollars at signing. The value of that deal fell sharply as internet stocks collapsed later that year. Silknet's eService suite became part of Kana's product line. Kana itself struggled through the downturn that followed.

cover.artwork: Spinning Cloth, Preparing Tea Leaves, Preparing Silk

tagline: Email on the Living Room TV
dek: WorldGate let people check email and browse the web on their TV, using the cable box they already had.
lede: WorldGate wanted people to read their email with a TV remote and a wireless keyboard. In 1999 most American homes had a television and a cable box, but far fewer had a personal computer. WorldGate's service ran through existing cable set-top boxes. It also let a TV show or ad link straight to a related website. WorldGate went public in April 1999, with cable operators as partners.

sections.heading: The Television Comes First
sections.body: The bet was that the television, ahead of the PC, would be most people's door to the internet. WorldGate's system did the heavy work on servers at the cable company. That let it run on boxes already in living rooms. Cable operators saw a way to sell a new service without new hardware in every home. It was an early try at the connected television that companies would attempt again in later decades.

sections.heading: Then Came Video Phones
sections.body: WorldGate priced its offering at $21 a share in April 1999, at the high point of enthusiasm for interactive TV. Interactive TV proved a hard sell. Cheap PCs and broadband pulled people toward computers instead. In the 2000s WorldGate shifted its focus to video phones. It stayed small and struggled financially. Watching and browsing on one screen returned years later, carried by smart TVs and streaming boxes.

tagline: Gigabit Switches, Built to Beat Cisco
dek: Extreme Networks brought gigabit speed to corporate networks, at a lower cost per port than older switches.
lede: Ethernet had just reached gigabit speeds, and Extreme Networks built switches to sell that speed for less. In 1999 corporate networks strained under new traffic from the web, email, and file sharing. Extreme's Summit and BlackDiamond lines used custom chips to switch traffic at full speed, at a lower cost per port than older designs. Extreme went public in April 1999, in the second wave of a networking boom.

sections.heading: Ethernet All the Way Up
sections.body: Gordon Stitt, Stephen Haddock, and Herb Schneider founded Extreme in 1996. The bet was that Ethernet would scale from the desktop to the network core. They also bet that a focused start-up could beat bigger rivals on speed and price. Extreme built its switches around custom chips that handled routing and switching in hardware. Customers ranged from universities to data centers. Extreme competed head on with Cisco and with other new switch makers.

sections.heading: Off to North Carolina
sections.body: Extreme priced its offering at $17 a share in April 1999. The stock rose sharply through 2000 before falling with the market. The company survived the crash and grew by acquisition, buying wireless and data center businesses from Motorola, Avaya, and Brocade. It moved its headquarters from Silicon Valley to North Carolina. Extreme remains a public company today, trading on the Nasdaq as EXTR.

dek: Claimsnet.com let small doctors' offices file insurance claims over the web, for faster payment and fewer errors.
lede: Claimsnet.com asked a small doctor's office for just two things: a web browser and an internet connection. Every visit to a doctor produced a form that had to be checked, coded, and sent to the right insurer. Large hospitals had expensive systems for this work. Many small practices still used paper. Claimsnet let them enter claims in a browser, then checked each claim and sent it on electronically. The Dallas company went public in April 1999.

sections.heading: Paperwork, Priced by the Claim
sections.body: The bet was that small medical offices would use the web to cut the cost and delay of filing claims. American healthcare had always run on paper, and in the 1990s insurance claims were among the heaviest piles. Large hospitals already had expensive systems to handle them. Smaller practices often still filed on paper. Claimsnet charged by the claim and promised faster payment with fewer errors.

sections.heading: Off the Nasdaq
sections.body: Claimsnet.com priced its offering at $8 a share in April 1999, selling 2,500,000 shares. The company stayed small. The healthcare internet market proved slower and more crowded than investors had hoped. The stock later moved off the Nasdaq to the over-the-counter market. Claimsnet kept working in claims processing as a small company. It never reached the scale its offering had promised.

fate: Taken private by its largest shareholders, 2008
dek: Critical Path ran email for internet providers, phone companies, and big businesses, so they could skip running it themselves.
lede: Critical Path sold email as a hosted service years before anyone called that cloud computing. In 1999 email was becoming the most important application on the internet, and running it well was hard. Internet providers, phone companies, and large businesses needed mail servers that could handle millions of accounts without failing. Critical Path ran those servers for them. Customers kept their own brand, and Critical Path handled the storage and spam. It went public in March 1999.

sections.heading: Paid by the Mailbox
sections.body: David Hayden founded Critical Path in San Francisco in 1997. The bet was that email was too important and too complex for most companies to run themselves. Critical Path built large data centers for mail and signed deals with carriers and portals. It was one of the first companies to sell email as a hosted service. Customers paid by the mailbox, so revenue grew with every new account.

sections.heading: A Scandal, Then Mergers
sections.body: Critical Path priced its offering at $24 a share in March 1999, and the stock soared through 2000. In 2001 an accounting scandal forced restatements, and several former employees were later convicted. The company survived and shifted to selling messaging software to carriers. Its major shareholders took it private in 2008. In 2010 it merged with Mirapoint, and in 2013 Openwave Messaging bought the combined company.

cover.theme: a mail stagecoach on the road

dek: iVillage gave women an online place to trade advice on health, parenting, money, and work.
lede: The web of 1999 was seen as a place built by and for young men, and iVillage's stock more than doubled on its first day anyway. Its sites and message boards covered parenting, health, careers, and relationships. Women used them to trade advice with each other. When it went public that March, iVillage was among the largest destinations for women online. It was also one of the most watched media start-ups in New York.

sections.heading: Community Before Content
sections.body: Candice Carpenter, Nancy Evans, and Robert Levitan founded iVillage in New York in 1995. The bet was that women would come online for community as much as for content. The founders built the site around message boards where members gave each other advice. Then they sold advertising and sponsorships to brands that wanted to reach those women. Early investors included America Online. That focus set iVillage apart from portals built for a general audience.

sections.heading: Women.com, Then NBC
sections.body: iVillage priced its offering at $24 a share in March 1999, and the stock more than doubled on its first day. Losses were heavy in the years that followed, and the share price fell sharply when the bubble burst. iVillage cut costs, bought its rival Women.com, and eventually turned a profit. By then its message boards had outlasted the hype. NBC Universal acquired the company in 2006 for about $600 million.

dek: Intraware let companies get business software over the internet, with every license tracked in one place.
lede: Intraware started as a software reseller, and the tool it built to track licenses outlived the rest of the business. Business software in 1999 still arrived in boxes, on CDs, with license keys printed on paper. Intraware, based in the San Francisco Bay Area, resold software from major vendors and delivered it over the internet. It went public in February 1999, betting that companies would download their software instead of unpacking it.

sections.heading: SubscribeNet Takes Over
sections.body: The bet was that software delivery and licensing were messy enough to be a business of their own. Intraware built a service called SubscribeNet. It let software makers deliver products and updates to customers and track who was entitled to what. Its customers included large companies that bought software from many vendors. Over time SubscribeNet became more important than the reselling business.

sections.heading: Four Dollars a Share
sections.body: Intraware priced its offering at $16 a share in February 1999. The stock rose in the boom and then fell hard. The company dropped reselling and focused on SubscribeNet, selling it to software makers as a service. In January 2009 Acresso Software, later renamed Flexera, acquired Intraware for $4.00 a share in cash, about $27 million in all. SubscribeNet lived on inside Flexera's licensing products.

dek: Vignette let big websites publish thousands of pages, change them daily, and tailor them to each visitor.
lede: Vignette's StoryServer built a web page only when a visitor asked for it, and it could build a different page for each visitor. In 1999 big websites were growing faster than anyone could update them by hand. Newspapers, retailers, and banks needed their editors to publish thousands of pages and change them daily. StoryServer kept the content in a database. Vignette went public in February 1999 as one of the stars of Austin's growing tech scene.

sections.heading: Software for Publishing Houses
sections.body: Ross Garber founded Vignette in Austin in 1995. The bet was that websites would become as complex as publishing houses and would need software to match. Vignette sold to media companies first, then to any business with a large website. It charged high license fees. Its product was expensive and complex. For a large website in 1999, there were few alternatives.

sections.heading: Billions, Then $310 Million
sections.body: Vignette priced its offering at $19 a share in February 1999, and the stock soared through the following year. Its market grew as every major company moved online. At its peak Vignette was worth billions of dollars. Then the market crashed, and cheaper content tools crowded in. Vignette shrank but stayed in business for a decade. Open Text acquired it in 2009 for about $310 million.

cover.artwork: Vignettes of Labor (Weaving, Fishing, Digging, Painting)

fate: Merged with WebMD, 1999; continued as WebMD
dek: Healtheon set out to connect doctors, insurers, and patients online and strip the paperwork out of American healthcare.
lede: Jim Clark had already co-founded Silicon Graphics and Netscape when he took on the most paper-bound industry in America. His third company, Healtheon, went after healthcare's claims, referrals, and approvals. They moved by fax and phone and cost huge sums. Healtheon wanted to connect every doctor, insurer, lab, and patient over the internet so those steps happened automatically. Its offering in February 1999 drew attention largely because of Clark's track record.

sections.heading: Too Many Players, Few Standards
sections.body: Jim Clark founded Healtheon in 1995. The bet was that the internet could take a large share of the waste out of healthcare administration. The company built software to check eligibility, submit claims, and handle referrals online. Progress was slower than planned. Healthcare had many players and few shared standards. Doctors, insurers, and hospitals each used different systems, and few saw a reason to change quickly.

sections.heading: Taking the WebMD Name
sections.body: Healtheon priced its offering at $8 a share in February 1999, and the stock rose sharply that spring. Later in 1999 it merged with WebMD and several other companies, and the combined business took the WebMD name. WebMD became the best-known consumer health site in America. Cutting paperwork remained a large part of the business. WebMD stayed a public company until it was taken private in 2017.

tagline: A Trade Magazine for Every Industry
dek: VerticalNet gave professionals in dozens of industries, from chemicals to food service, an online place to meet and trade.
lede: VerticalNet ran websites for industries as narrow as water treatment, and at its peak Wall Street valued it in the billions. In 1999 investors believed the biggest internet opportunity lay in trade between businesses. VerticalNet ran dozens of industry sites, each a community with news, product listings, and job boards. It earned money from advertising and from deals between suppliers and buyers. It went public in February 1999 as the leading example of business-to-business commerce.

sections.heading: Content First, Then Markets
sections.body: Michael McNulty and Douglas Alexander founded VerticalNet in Pennsylvania in 1995. The bet was that each industry would gather online in its own vertical community. VerticalNet built or bought sites for fields such as water treatment, semiconductors, and food service. Each community gave suppliers a focused audience and gave buyers a place to compare options. The plan was to start with content and grow into trading marketplaces once buyers and sellers were in one place.

sections.heading: The Boom, Then BravoSolution
sections.body: VerticalNet priced its offering at $16 a share in February 1999, and its stock rose many times over within a year. At its peak the company was worth billions of dollars. When the business-to-business bubble burst in 2000, it sold most of its communities. It turned to procurement software, the tools companies use to manage their buying. BravoSolution acquired VerticalNet in 2008.

cover.artwork: Prairie School Skyscraper, Chicago, Illinois, Perspective

dek: Tut Systems let hotels and apartment buildings offer fast internet over the phone wiring already inside their walls.
lede: With Tut Systems' equipment, a hotel could offer guests internet access without pulling a single new cable. Apartment buildings, hotels, and campuses were full of copper wire installed for telephones. Tut built products that let that wiring carry fast data as well. It also worked on home networking over phone lines. Tut went public in January 1999, as everyone looked for ways to reach the last few hundred feet.

sections.heading: The Wires Already There
sections.body: The bet was that the wires already in place were worth more than people thought. Rewiring a building was costly and slow. Tut's equipment worked with what was already there. That saved time and money in the rush to wire buildings for the internet. Tut sold to building owners, service providers, and phone companies that wanted to offer broadband in multi-tenant buildings. Property owners could add a service without tearing open walls.

sections.heading: From Building Wires to Video
sections.body: Tut priced its offering at $18 a share in January 1999. The stock rose through the boom and collapsed in 2000 and 2001. The company shifted to video processing systems for telecom carriers offering television over broadband. In 2005 it bought Copper Mountain Networks. Motorola acquired Tut Systems in 2007. By then Tut sold video gear to telecom carriers, far from its roots in building wiring.

cover.artwork: Ostracon with a Drawing of a King

dek: Covad sold fast DSL internet across the country over phone lines it rented from the old Bell companies.
lede: Covad's name came from "copper value added," and every foot of that copper belonged to someone else. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 forced the old Bell phone companies to rent their lines to competitors. Covad was one of the boldest companies to take up the offer. It installed DSL equipment in central offices across the country and sold fast internet, mostly through internet providers. When Covad went public in January 1999, it was building one of the largest DSL networks in the United States.

sections.heading: First Into Every Market
sections.body: Charles McMinn, a Silicon Valley executive, co-founded Covad in 1996. The bet was that the regulated phone network could become a platform for new broadband carriers. Covad rented the lines and put its own DSL gear at the phone company's end. It raced to be first into the most markets. It spent heavily on equipment and staff before most customers had signed up. The plan was to win the market before the Bell companies could respond.

sections.heading: Chapter 11, Then Platinum
sections.body: Covad priced its offering at $18 a share in January 1999, and its stock rose steeply through the year. The pace was hard to sustain. Disputes with the Bell companies, unpaid bills from failing internet providers, and the telecom crash pushed Covad into Chapter 11 in 2001. It emerged and kept operating. Platinum Equity acquired it in 2008, and its network served business customers for years after.

cover.theme: a road lined with telegraph poles (copper lines)
cover.artwork: Tree-Lined Road with Houses and Telegraph Poles in Distance

dek: Artificial Life sold software bots that chatted with website visitors, guided shoppers, and fetched information.
lede: Artificial Life was selling chatbots in 1998, decades before they became common. Its software "robots" could answer questions on a website, guide shoppers, or search for information on a user's behalf. The ideas drew on research in artificial intelligence and software agents. The company was small and based in Boston, and its founder had roots in German AI research. It went public in December 1998, as interest in the web was surging.

sections.heading: Bots for Every Website
sections.body: Eberhard Schoneburg founded the company. The bet was that websites would need intelligent assistants for their visitors, and that companies would license software agents to provide them. Artificial Life built bots for customer service, shopping, and information retrieval. The technology was early. Its products were limited by what software of the day could understand. They were early steps toward the chatbots and virtual assistants that later became common.

sections.heading: From Boston to Hong Kong
sections.body: Artificial Life priced its offering at $8.50 a share in December 1998. Its stock began trading on the Nasdaq SmallCap Market on December 18, under the symbol ALIF. The company never grew large, and the dot-com crash hit it hard. It later moved its base to Hong Kong and turned to mobile games and applications. In its later years, its shares traded on the over-the-counter market.

cover.artwork: Large wind-up automaton of Asahina Saburo

tagline: The End of the Paper Expense Report
dek: Concur let employees file expense reports online and get them approved fast, then added business travel booking.
lede: Concur bet its future on the expense report, the dull chore at the end of every business trip. In the 1990s that report was usually a paper form or a spreadsheet, checked by hand in a finance office. Concur sold software that moved the process online. Employees could file expenses, and managers could approve them quickly. When it went public in December 1998, Concur was a small company in the Seattle area. Sixteen years later, SAP paid about $8.3 billion for it.

sections.heading: A Chore Every Company Shares
sections.body: Steve Singh, Rajeev Singh, and Mike Hilton founded the company in 1993. The bet was that expense reporting was a costly, error-prone task that every company shared. Large companies with many traveling employees were the natural first customers. Concur first sold software that customers installed themselves. Then it moved to delivering the software over the internet. That shift made it one of the early successes of software as a service.

sections.heading: Outtask, Then SAP
sections.body: Concur priced its offering at $12.50 a share in December 1998. The stock fell hard after 2000, and the company nearly ran out of room. It survived by moving to a subscription service. Later it added travel booking through its purchase of Outtask. Concur grew into the standard tool for business travel and expenses. SAP acquired it in 2014 for about $8.3 billion, one of the largest software deals of that year.

tagline: The Yellow Pages Behind the Portals
dek: InfoSpace supplied directories, maps, search, and news to other websites and phones, under those companies' own brands.
lede: InfoSpace's services ran on other companies' websites, under other companies' names. In 1998 many sites wanted yellow pages, white pages, maps, and news, but few wanted to build them. InfoSpace supplied those services, and the sites ran them under their own brands. It was part of the plumbing behind many portals. When it went public in December 1998, InfoSpace was a young Seattle-area company growing fast on deals with major websites and carriers.

sections.heading: Behind the Scenes on Purpose
sections.body: Naveen Jain, a former Microsoft manager, founded InfoSpace in 1996. The bet was to stay behind the scenes, licensing content and services to sites that already had users. InfoSpace earned money from advertising and fees as those sites grew. This model kept costs low and let the company grow quickly through partnerships. Later it supplied similar services to wireless carriers, as phones began to reach the internet.

sections.heading: Dogpile, Blucora, Avantax
sections.body: InfoSpace priced its offering at $15 a share in December 1998, and the stock rose dramatically. By early 2000 it was among the most valuable internet companies. Then it lost most of that value. It bought Go2Net in 2000, and lawsuits and losses followed. InfoSpace later focused on search through its Dogpile brand. It renamed itself Blucora in 2012 and moved into tax and wealth services. In 2023 Blucora took a new name, Avantax.

cover.theme: the constellation Leo from a book of stars (a directory)
cover.artwork: The Constellation Leo, folio probably from the Kitab suwar al-kawakib al-thabita (Book of the Images of the Fixed Stars)

tagline: Six Hundred Percent in a Day
dek: theglobe.com gave early web users free home pages, chat rooms, and forums, years before social networks.
lede: On its first day of trading, theglobe.com's stock rose more than 600 percent, a record for a first day. The company began as a project of two Cornell University students who saw the web as a place to meet people. It offered free personal home pages, chat rooms, and forums, years before social networks became a business. By late 1998 it had millions of members and a New York headquarters. Its offering that November became a defining moment of the dot-com era.

sections.heading: Two Cornell Students
sections.body: Stephan Paternot and Todd Krizelman started the company while they were students at Cornell. The bet was that online communities would draw huge audiences, and that advertisers would pay to reach them. theglobe.com grew by giving users tools to publish and connect. It also bought other community and gaming sites. Its members were young, and many were building their first web page.

sections.heading: A Symbol of Excess
sections.body: theglobe.com priced its offering at $9 a share on November 13, 1998. That record first-day jump made it a symbol of the era's excess. Advertising revenue failed to keep up with costs, and the stock collapsed in 2000 and 2001. In the years that followed, the company sold or closed most of its businesses. Its founders moved on to other ventures.

dek: eBay let anyone sell nearly anything to buyers across the country, through online auctions.
lede: eBay owned no inventory and shipped nothing, and in 1998 it was one of the few internet companies that turned a profit. Collectors traded toys, coins, and comics on the site. Ordinary people sold things from their attics to strangers who paid by mailed check. eBay ran the auctions and charged a fee for each listing and each sale. It went public in September 1998.

sections.heading: AuctionWeb and Feedback
sections.body: Pierre Omidyar, a software engineer, launched the site as AuctionWeb in 1995 from his apartment in the San Francisco Bay Area. The bet was that people would trust each other to trade if they had a fair market and a way to rate one another. eBay's feedback system let buyers and sellers build reputations. Collectors made up the earliest community. Their enthusiasm drew in everyone else, and the site grew by word of mouth.

sections.heading: PayPal In, PayPal Out
sections.body: eBay priced its offering at $18 a share in September 1998, and the stock nearly tripled on its first day. Under Meg Whitman, eBay grew into a global marketplace and a pillar of online commerce. It bought PayPal in 2002 and spun it off in 2015. Along the way it grew far beyond collectibles, into new and used goods of every kind. eBay remains a public company today, trading on the Nasdaq as EBAY.

fate: Acquired by WPP as 24/7 Real Media, 2007 ($649M)
tagline: A TV Network Made of Websites
dek: 24/7 Media sold ads across many websites at once, for sites too small to sell their own.
lede: 24/7 Media packaged the web's small sites the way a television network packages its stations. In 1998 thousands of websites had audiences but no sales staff to sell ads. Advertisers did not want to call each site one by one. 24/7 Media solved both problems. It gathered many sites into a network, sold ad space across all of them, and served the ads through its own technology. It went public in New York in August 1998.

sections.heading: The Long Tail, Packaged
sections.body: The bet was that the web's long tail of sites could be packaged and sold like a television network. 24/7 Media signed up publishers and split ad revenue with them. It used targeting tools to place ads where they would perform. Each new site made the network more useful to advertisers. It competed with DoubleClick and other networks for both advertisers and publishers, as online advertising grew into a real industry.

sections.heading: Real Media, Then WPP
sections.body: 24/7 Media priced its offering at $14 a share in August 1998. The stock rose through the boom. Then online ad spending collapsed in 2000 and 2001, and the stock fell sharply. In 2001 the company merged with Real Media and became 24/7 Real Media. WPP acquired it in 2007 for about $649 million. The deal put the network inside one of the world's largest advertising groups.

cover.theme: the moon at night (around the clock)

dek: Digital River ran online stores for software makers and other brands, handling payment, fraud, taxes, and downloads.
lede: Digital River ran the online stores of many large software brands, out of sight behind their names. In 1998 software still sold mostly in boxes on store shelves. The Minneapolis company believed it would soon arrive over the internet. It built and ran stores for software publishers, handled payments, and delivered the software as a download. It also ran a network of resellers that sold those products on their own sites. Digital River went public in August 1998.

sections.heading: Handing Off the Hard Parts
sections.body: Joel Ronning founded Digital River in 1994. The bet was that software makers would rather hand off e-commerce than build it, and that downloads would replace boxes. Digital River took a cut of each sale and handled the hard parts: payment, fraud, taxes, and delivery. Publishers got a ready-made store without building one themselves. Later it served game makers, electronics brands, and other companies selling directly online.

sections.heading: Saved by Transactions, Then Shut
sections.body: Digital River priced its offering at $8.50 a share in August 1998, and the stock rose sharply in the boom. It survived the crash because its revenue came from transactions. Siris Capital took Digital River private in 2015 for about $840 million. In 2024 it stopped paying many of the merchants whose software it sold. In early 2025 it closed its Minnesota offices and began winding down its operations.

dek: Broadcast.com let people hear live radio, sports, and events over the internet, years before broadband.
lede: Broadcast.com made Mark Cuban a billionaire by streaming crackly audio to people on dial-up modems. It carried hundreds of radio stations, college and professional sports, press conferences, and live events. Fans could listen to hometown games from anywhere. In 1998 most people still reached the internet by dial-up, and streaming audio was unreliable. The Dallas company streamed it anyway. It went public in July 1998 and became one of the defining stocks of the early internet boom.

sections.heading: AudioNet Becomes Broadcast.com
sections.body: The company began as AudioNet, started by Chris Jaeb in 1995. Todd Wagner and Mark Cuban joined soon after and turned it into Broadcast.com. The bet was that the internet would become a broadcast medium, like radio and television before it. Whoever controlled the content and the servers would win. Broadcast.com earned money from advertising and from companies that paid to stream their own events.

sections.heading: Yahoo's $5.7 Billion Purchase
sections.body: Broadcast.com priced its offering at $18 a share in July 1998, and the stock rose about 250 percent on its first day. Less than a year later, Yahoo agreed to buy the company in a stock deal worth about $5.7 billion. The company was about four years old. The deal made Mark Cuban a billionaire. Yahoo struggled to make the business work, and within a few years the service had faded.

dek: Broadcom designed the chips inside cable modems and set-top boxes that brought broadband into homes.
lede: Broadcom began with a UCLA professor and his former student, and its name survived a $37 billion takeover. In 1998 the race to bring broadband into homes depended on chips that could send data over cable TV lines and phone wires. Broadcom designed many of them. Its chips sat inside cable modems, digital set-top boxes, and networking gear. Broadcom owned no factories. It designed chips and paid others to make them. It went public in April 1998.

sections.heading: A System on a Chip
sections.body: Henry Samueli, a UCLA professor, and Henry Nicholas, his former student, founded Broadcom in 1991. The bet was that broadband would need complete systems on a chip, with many functions combined in one piece of silicon. That approach cut costs for equipment makers. It made Broadcom a key supplier for cable modems and Ethernet. Broadcom also built a reputation for hiring top engineers and for aggressive competition.

sections.heading: Bought, Then Renamed Broadcom
sections.body: Broadcom priced its offering at $24 a share in April 1998, and the stock soared with the broadband boom. It grew into one of the largest chip companies in the world, adding Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and networking chips. In 2016 Avago Technologies acquired Broadcom for about $37 billion. It was one of the largest deals in the history of the chip industry. The combined company took the Broadcom name.

dek: ISS found the weak spots in company networks and caught attacks while they were happening.
lede: Internet Security Systems began as a program a Georgia Tech student wrote to find holes in networks. By 1998 companies were connecting to the internet faster than they could secure themselves. Firewalls kept some threats out. Few tools could find weak spots inside or spot an attack in progress. The Atlanta company sold both. Its scanners checked networks for known holes, and its RealSecure product watched traffic for signs of attack. It went public in March 1998 as ISS Group.

sections.heading: Security Never Finishes
sections.body: Christopher Klaus wrote the first version of Internet Scanner while he was a student at Georgia Tech. He founded ISS in 1994. The bet was that security would become a constant process instead of a one-time setup. ISS built a research team that tracked new vulnerabilities and updated its products to find them. That team, later called X-Force, became one of the best-known names in security. Customers included banks, government agencies, and large corporations.

sections.heading: X-Force Joins IBM
sections.body: ISS priced its offering at $22 a share in March 1998, and its stock rose through the internet boom. The company grew into one of the largest pure security vendors and added managed security services. In 2006 IBM bought ISS for about $1.3 billion, or $28 a share in cash. ISS became part of IBM's security services business. IBM kept the X-Force research service running for its customers.

dek: DoubleClick picked which banner ad each web visitor saw, and counted every view and click for advertisers.
lede: DoubleClick counted every banner ad it showed and every click it got, a kind of proof print and television could never give advertisers. By early 1998 banner ads paid the bills for much of the web, but placing them was crude. DoubleClick ran the servers that delivered ads to thousands of sites. It used data about each visit to pick the ad, targeting people by interest, location, or time of day. The New York company went public in February 1998.

sections.heading: Advertising You Could Measure
sections.body: Kevin O'Connor and Dwight Merriman founded DoubleClick in 1996. The bet was that technology could make web advertising measurable in a way print and television never were. DoubleClick sold ads across a network of sites. It also licensed its ad-serving tools to large publishers. Its system counted every impression and every click. By its offering, DoubleClick was the leading name in online advertising.

sections.heading: A Privacy Uproar, Then Google
sections.body: DoubleClick priced its offering at $17 a share in February 1998, and the stock rose dramatically through 1999. In 2000 its plan to merge web data with offline customer records set off a privacy uproar. Hellman & Friedman took the company private in 2005. Google acquired DoubleClick in 2008 for about $3.1 billion. DoubleClick's ad tools became a core part of Google's advertising business.

cover.artwork: The Twin Brothers Ludwig and Emil Schulthess

dek: VeriSign proved to shoppers that a website was genuine, so they could type in a credit card without fear.
lede: The little padlock in a browser's address bar rested on certificates that VeriSign issued. In 1998 shoppers were nervous about typing a credit card number into a website. Encryption could protect the data in transit. People also needed proof that the site was genuine. VeriSign provided that proof, and browsers checked it automatically. When VeriSign went public in January 1998, it was becoming a trusted third party for the whole web.

sections.heading: A Notary for the Web
sections.body: VeriSign was spun out of RSA Data Security in 1995, with Jim Bidzos, RSA's leader, as its founding force. The bet was that online trust would need a neutral authority, much like a notary. VeriSign checked the identity of businesses and signed their certificates. Browsers came preloaded to trust VeriSign's signature. That trust put VeriSign at the center of online commerce.

sections.heading: Keeper of .com
sections.body: VeriSign priced its offering at $14 a share in January 1998, and the stock rose hugely in the boom. In 2000 it bought Network Solutions, which ran the registry for .com and .net domain names. VeriSign later sold its certificate business to Symantec and kept the registry. It remains a public company today. Its registry still handles every .com address on the internet.

cover.theme: a woman sealing a letter (trust and identity)

tagline: A Checkup for the Corporate Network
dek: Concord Communications showed companies how well their networks were running, in reports that non-experts could read.
lede: Concord Communications called its software Network Health, and it worked like a regular checkup for a corporate network. In 1997 those networks were growing large and complex, and the people who ran them had little insight into how well they worked. Network Health gathered data from routers, switches, and servers. It turned that data into clear reports on traffic, errors, and capacity. Managers could see trouble coming and plan upgrades. The Massachusetts company went public in October 1997.

sections.heading: Reports Anyone Could Read
sections.body: The bet was that networks had become critical to business, and that managers would pay for clear measures of their health. Concord's software worked with equipment from many vendors. It produced reports that non-specialists could read. It sold to large companies, and to service providers that needed to prove they met their promises to customers. It sold licenses and support, and its customers renewed year after year.

sections.heading: Empire, Aprisma, Then CA
sections.body: Concord priced its offering at $14 a share in October 1997. The offering gave it the money to grow during the boom years. It bought Empire Technologies and Aprisma to widen its products. Concord stayed a steady software maker that sold to network managers and kept its focus on a single problem it understood well. Computer Associates acquired Concord in 2005, and its tools became part of CA's network management line.

cover.artwork: View of the Battle Ground at Concord, Massachusetts

dek: Logility let manufacturers and retailers forecast demand, so they kept less stock sitting idle without running out.
lede: Logility's software went looking for the money that hid in a company's warehouses. Too much stock tied up cash, and too little lost sales. Logility forecast demand, planned inventory, and coordinated transport across a company's suppliers and warehouses. It was a unit of American Software, an Atlanta company. In October 1997 American Software sold part of Logility to the public in an offering and kept majority control.

sections.heading: A Market of Its Own
sections.body: In the 1990s manufacturers and retailers were learning how much of their cost hid in the supply chain. The bet was that supply chain planning was a large market of its own, separate from general business software. Logility sold to consumer goods makers, distributors, and retailers. Its tools let planners look ahead, test scenarios, and share forecasts with partners. That cut waste and improved service for companies that moved large volumes of goods.

sections.heading: Back Home, Then Aptean
sections.body: Logility priced its offering at $14.50 a share in October 1997 and sold 2.2 million shares. It stayed a small public company, with American Software as its controlling owner. In 2009 American Software bought the shares it did not already own and took Logility back in-house. American Software later took the Logility name for itself. In April 2025 Aptean bought the company for $14.30 a share in cash.

dek: 8x8 made chips that squeezed video onto phone lines, then turned itself into an internet phone company.
lede: 8x8 built chips to put your face on a phone call, a decade before anyone wanted one. The Silicon Valley company designed processors that squeezed video and audio down small enough to travel over ordinary phone lines. Its chips went into videophones and conference-room systems. When it went public in July 1997, 8x8 was a small semiconductor maker betting that people would want to see each other when they called.

sections.heading: Squeezing Video Through Narrow Pipes
sections.body: Joe Parkinson and Chi-Ping Hsu founded the company in 1987. The bet was that compression was the key to sending rich media through narrow pipes. 8x8 designed chips and complete systems for video calling. It would change its business more than once. The first change came as the internet grew, when the company saw that voice and video calls could run over data networks as well as phone lines.

sections.heading: Close to Broke, Then Cloud
sections.body: 8x8 priced its offering at $6.50 a share in July 1997 and sold 4,140,000 shares. The stock rose in the boom and fell in the crash, when the company came close to running out of money. 8x8 remade itself as a service provider, selling internet phone service to small businesses. It grew into a cloud communications company. 8x8 remains publicly traded today, under the symbol EGHT.

dek: Amazon sold books online from a catalog bigger than any physical store could hold.
lede: Amazon was a bookstore with no stores, and it planned to keep losing money in order to grow. It sold books through a website, shipped them from a warehouse in Seattle, and claimed a catalog of more than a million titles. Few people bought anything online yet, and many doubted they ever would. Amazon went public in May 1997 with an offering that was modest by later standards. It called itself Earth's Biggest Bookstore.

sections.heading: Leaving the Hedge Fund
sections.body: Jeff Bezos left a hedge fund job in New York in 1994 and drove west to start the company. He chose books because there were millions of titles, too many for any shop to stock. The bet was that the web's unlimited shelf would beat physical stores on selection. Customers would reward low prices and convenience. Bezos told investors to expect a long wait for profits.

sections.heading: The Kindle and the Cloud
sections.body: Amazon priced its offering at $18 a share in May 1997. It added music and video, then almost everything else. It opened its site to other sellers and survived the dot-com crash. It launched Prime, the Kindle, and Amazon Web Services, which turned its own computing systems into a business. Amazon remains a public company today, one of the largest in the world, trading on the Nasdaq as AMZN.

dek: Go2Net's MetaCrawler searched many search engines at once, so people saw more of the web from one query.
lede: Go2Net's MetaCrawler began as a research project at the University of Washington. In 1997 the web had many search engines, and each covered only part of it. A search on one engine could miss pages that another found. MetaCrawler sent a single query to several engines at once, then combined the results. The Seattle company added other sites and services around it. Go2Net went public in April 1997, early in the internet boom, with a small offering.

sections.heading: A Layer on Top
sections.body: Russell Horowitz founded Go2Net in 1996. The bet was that the web needed a layer on top of existing tools, one that saved people time by gathering results into one page. Go2Net licensed MetaCrawler from the University of Washington and made it part of its service in March 1997. It earned money from advertising on its growing network of sites. That network also included sites built around games and finance.

sections.heading: Paul Allen, Then InfoSpace
sections.body: Go2Net priced its offering at $8 a share in April 1997, selling 1,600,000 shares. The stock rose many times over during the boom, with a lift from an investment by Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures. In 2000 Go2Net merged with InfoSpace in a stock deal worth about $4 billion at announcement. It was one of the final big deals of the boom. MetaCrawler and Dogpile, which Go2Net had bought, lived on under InfoSpace.

cover.theme: a fisherman mending a net (the net)

dek: CNET explained computers and the internet to first-time buyers, through cable TV shows and websites full of reviews.
lede: CNET built its brand with cable television shows about computers, then sent the audience to its websites. In 1996 the computer industry was booming, and millions of people were buying their first PC or going online for the first time. CNET set out to explain it all. Its websites offered news, reviews, and software downloads. The San Francisco company went public in July 1996, one of the first media companies built for the internet age.

sections.heading: Download.com and News.com
sections.body: Halsey Minor founded CNET in 1992, and Shelby Bonnie joined him early and later ran the company. The bet was that technology was becoming a mainstream subject, worthy of its own network. CNET used television to build its brand and the web to reach readers directly. Its sites, including Download.com and News.com, became regular stops for computer users. It sold advertising to the technology companies its readers followed.

sections.heading: CBS, Red Ventures, Ziff Davis
sections.body: CNET priced its offering at $16 a share in July 1996. It grew through the boom and bought the comparison shopping site mySimon and the media company ZDNet. It survived the crash as one of the largest web publishers. CBS acquired CNET in 2008 for about $1.8 billion. In 2020 Red Ventures bought it for $500 million. In 2024 Ziff Davis agreed to buy CNET for about $100 million.

dek: A.D.A.M. let students peel back the human body on a computer screen, layer by layer, from skin to bone.
lede: A.D.A.M. stood for Animated Dissection of Anatomy for Medicine, and its software let anyone dissect a body on a personal computer. Students peeled back layers of anatomy, from skin to bone. The CD-ROM was the new medium of learning, and the Atlanta company sold its discs to schools, medical students, and families. It went public in November 1995, just as the web began to draw attention away from CD-ROMs.

sections.heading: Better Than a Textbook
sections.body: A.D.A.M. was founded in Atlanta in 1990. The bet was that detailed medical illustration, delivered by computer, could teach anatomy better than textbooks. The company built a large library of accurate images and animations. It sold versions for medical schools and simpler ones for home and school use. The images became its main asset. The company reused them for decades in new formats.

sections.heading: From CD-ROM to Ebix
sections.body: A.D.A.M. priced its offering at $12 a share and completed it on November 10, 1995. As CD-ROMs faded, the company turned its library into online health content. It licensed that content to hospitals, health sites, and insurers. It later added benefits technology for employers. Its anatomy library outlived the medium it was built for. In 2011 Ebix, the Atlanta insurance software company, acquired A.D.A.M. for about $66 million.
